title: Afternoon ambush: reading storm towers
teaches: Will today’s cumulus puffs erupt into a thunderstorm, and when should you get indoors? Latent heat and conditional instability, castle turrets at breakfast, the tropopause anvil, the gust front, and the 30–30 lightning rule.

blocks.title: The big ideas of this lesson
points: Inside a cloud, condensing water vapour releases **latent heat**, so rising cloudy air cools at only about 5 °C per kilometre (3 °F per 1,000 feet) instead of 10 °C. That extra warmth is why a cumulus heap, once formed, can surge upward.

Track the three growth stages of cumulus: flattened **humilis** (fair weather), **mediocris** (as tall as it is wide), and towering **congestus** (a warning if seen by midday). Miniature castle turrets on morning altocumulus (**castellanus**) warn that the middle sky is already unstable.
A tower that climbs all the way to the **tropopause** (10–12 km up) spreads out into an icy anvil: a **cumulonimbus**, or thunderstorm. A single storm cell lives for about an hour.
A sudden blast of cool, gusty wind on a hot afternoon is the storm’s cold downdraught arriving—the **gust front**—typically 5 to 15 minutes ahead of the downpour and lightning.

Count the seconds from lightning flash to thunder: divide by 3 for kilometres (or by 5 for miles). Under 30 seconds means the storm is within 10 km—get indoors and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder (**the 30–30 rule**).

blocks.text: In Lesson 1, afternoon cumulus puffs stayed small and harmless because stable air aloft stopped their climb. On some summer days, nothing stops them. By midday the puffs have swollen into cauliflower towers, and by mid-afternoon one of them is hurling lightning across the valley. This lesson shows how to spot that buildup early—and how to know when to head indoors.

Why does a rising thermal suddenly gain a second wind once it condenses into a cloud? When liquid water evaporates, it absorbs heat from its surroundings—which is why evaporating sweat cools your skin. When water vapour condenses back into liquid droplets inside a rising cloud, it releases that exact same stored heat back into the air. Meteorologists call this **latent heat** (from the Latin for 'hidden'). That released heat warms the cloudy parcel from within, slowing its cooling rate from 10 °C per kilometre down to roughly 5 °C per kilometre.[^moist-rate]

Whether the cloudy parcel keeps climbing still depends on how its cooling rate compares with the surrounding sky. Above the lowest kilometre or two, the atmosphere typically cools by 6 to 7 °C per kilometre. A dry thermal cooling at 10 °C per kilometre quickly becomes colder than that surrounding air and stalls. A cloudy thermal cooling at 5 °C per kilometre, however, stays *warmer* than that exact same 6–7 °C/km environment—so its buoyancy grows with every metre it climbs, driving it upward into billowing cauliflower towers.[^conditional]

blocks.title: The stability test, in full
points: Compare two cooling rates: how fast the **surrounding sky** gets colder with height, and how fast a **rising parcel** cools.
A clear (dry) parcel cools at 10 °C per kilometre; a cloudy parcel cools at only about 5 °C per kilometre because condensing vapour releases latent heat.

Whenever the surrounding sky cools *faster* than the parcel, the parcel stays warmer than its neighbours and accelerates upward (**unstable**). Whenever the sky cools *more slowly*, the parcel becomes colder than its neighbours and sinks back (**stable**).
An atmosphere that cools at 6 to 7 °C per kilometre is stable for clear air (slower than 10) but unstable for cloudy air (faster than 5)—allowing cumulus clouds to tower upward once they condense.

blocks.caption: Temperature by height: the air around, and a bubble before and after it turns to cloud.

blocks.text: Three controls govern how tall a cumulus heap can grow. First, **surface heating** sets the starting temperature of rising thermals. Second, low-level **moisture** sets the altitude of the cloud base, determining how early the rising parcel switches to the slower 5 °C/km cloudy cooling rate. Third, a warm [[inversion|env]] layer aloft can cap the climb completely. When a rising cloud top pokes into a strong inversion, even latent heat cannot keep the parcel warmer than the warm lid around it, and the cloud flattens out.

Observers divide cumulus into three species that track this vertical growth. **Cumulus humilis** is flattened—wider than it is tall—and marks fair weather. **Cumulus mediocris** grows roughly as tall as it is wide, with modest vertical bulges. **Cumulus congestus** (or *towering cumulus*) surges into tall, sharp-edged cauliflower chimneys much taller than they are wide. Seeing congestus towers already building by late morning or midday is a clear warning that full thunderstorms may erupt by afternoon.

Sometimes the middle floor gives an even earlier warning around breakfast. If you spot rows of middle-level altocumulus sprouting miniature, narrow turrets like battlements on a castle, you are looking at **altocumulus castellanus**. Those turrets show that latent heat is already driving narrow updraughts through an unstable middle sky (cooling faster than 5 °C/km). Once afternoon sunshine heats the ground below, surface thermals can link up with that middle-level instability and rocket straight into thunderstorms.

Forecasters and glider pilots diagnose this vertical profile using an upper-air chart called a **sounding**. Twice a day, weather stations worldwide release helium or hydrogen balloons carrying a compact instrument package that radios back temperature, humidity, and wind readings every few seconds as it climbs.[^radiosonde]

In the sounding diagram below, **temperature runs along the bottom** (warmer to the right) and **altitude runs up the left side**. The solid violet curve shows the surrounding air temperature measured by the balloon (while the dashed violet curve shows the cooler dawn profile before surface heating). The teal curve tracks the dew point, and the orange curve follows a rising surface parcel—cooling at 10 °C/km up to the cloud base, then bending steeper to cool at ~5 °C/km inside the cloud. Wherever the violet environment curve tilts steeply to the left, the sky cools rapidly with height. At any altitude where the orange parcel curve sits to the *right* of the violet environment curve, the parcel is warmer than the surrounding sky and accelerates upward; where the two curves cross again at the top, the parcel loses its buoyancy and stops.[^cape]

blocks.caption: A summer day over farm country, with a warm layer a couple of kilometres up.
blocks.task: Grow a cumulus congestus: a tower several kilometres tall.

blocks.text: When no middle-level inversion caps a growing congestus tower, its updraught can surge all the way to the top of the troposphere—about 10 to 12 kilometres up in mid-latitudes. Throughout the troposphere, the air generally gets colder with altitude because it is warmed primarily from the ground up. Around 10 to 12 kilometres, however, that cooling abruptly stops.

Above that level sits the **stratosphere**, which is heated from above by the **ozone layer**. High in the stratosphere, intense solar ultraviolet light splits ordinary oxygen molecules (O₂) into single atoms that recombine with O₂ to form ozone (O₃). Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts it into heat, causing the stratosphere to grow warmer with altitude.

The boundary where temperature stops falling with height and starts rising is the **tropopause**. Because the stratosphere warms with height, the tropopause acts as a giant, permanent temperature inversion—a ceiling across the top of the weather that halts rising storm towers.

blocks.caption: Temperature by height, from the ground into the stratosphere.

blocks.text: When a vigorous storm updraught slams into the stable tropopause, the rising air cannot climb much further and fans out horizontally beneath the ceiling like smoke hitting a flat roof.[^overshooting] At 10 to 12 kilometres up, temperatures sit below −50 °C, so the cloud top is completely frozen; upper-level winds draw those spreading ice crystals downwind into a vast, flat-topped **anvil** (*incus*) with silky, fibrous edges. Once the top of a towering heap freezes into fibrous ice and heavy rain begins falling from its base, the cloud has graduated from cumulus congestus to **cumulonimbus**—a thunderstorm.

In the interactive sounding below, an **instability** slider lets you adjust how rapidly the upper troposphere cools with height. Tilting the violet environment line further left widens the temperature gap between the rising cloudy parcel (orange) and the surrounding air, fueling faster updraughts that punch all the way to the tropopause.

blocks.caption: The same day, with the instability control added.
blocks.task: Remove the lid and make the air unstable enough to grow a cumulonimbus.

blocks.text: An ordinary single-cell thunderstorm goes through a three-stage life cycle lasting about 45 to 60 minutes.

blocks.caption: One thunderstorm cell, from first heap to last shower.
blocks.task: Guess what ends the storm, then run it to the end of its life.

blocks.text: During the **developing stage** (or cumulus stage), the tower is driven entirely by warm, buoyant updraughts carrying humid surface air skyward. No rain reaches the ground yet as condensing water and ice accumulate aloft.

The **mature stage** begins when the load of rain and ice grows too heavy for the updraught to hold up and starts plunging toward the ground. Inside powerful updraughts, small ice pellets get tossed up and down through dense zones of supercooled liquid droplets that freeze onto them in layers like an onion, building **hailstones** until they grow heavy enough to fall out.

As heavy rain and hail plunge earthward, they drag surrounding air down with them. At the same time, dry mid-level air mixes into the edges of the rain shaft and evaporates part of the falling water, absorbing latent heat and chilling the air pocket. Colder and denser than its surroundings, this chilled air plunges to the ground as a strong **downdraught**. During its mature stage, the storm runs a warm updraught and a cold downdraught side by side—unleashing its heaviest downpours, hail, frequent lightning, and violent wind gusts.

Finally, in the **dissipating stage**, the cold downdraught spreads out across the ground in all directions, undercutting and choking off the warm, humid inflow that fed the updraught. Starved of fuel from below, the updraught collapses and the lower tower rains itself out, often leaving an orphaned ice anvil drifting high overhead.

That spreading pool of rain-cooled air gives you an unmistakable warning on the ground. On a hot, sticky afternoon, a sudden blast of cool, gusty wind blowing out from under a dark storm tower—often kicking up swirling dust—is the leading edge of the downdraught: the **gust front**. Because the cold outflow races ahead of the rain shaft, the gust front usually hits **5 to 15 minutes** before the downpour and overhead lightning arrive. When the air suddenly turns cool and blustery beneath a darkening sky, head indoors immediately.

Inside the turbulent middle levels of a cumulonimbus (between about −10 °C and −25 °C), rising ice crystals, falling pellets of soft hail (*graupel*), and supercooled droplets constantly slam into one another. Just as rubbing a balloon against your hair transfers electrons from one surface to the other, collisions between tiny ice crystals and heavier graupel pellets transfer electric charge.

Each collision leaves the tiny, rising ice crystals with a slight positive charge and the heavier, falling graupel pellets with a negative charge. The storm’s updraught sweeps the lightweight, positively charged ice crystals high into the anvil, while gravity pulls the negatively charged graupel into the middle and lower belly of the cloud—turning the thunderstorm into a giant electrostatic battery.

blocks.caption: Where a thunderstorm keeps its charge.

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the strong negative charge in the lower cloud repels electrons in the ground directly beneath the storm, leaving the ground surface positively charged. Once the electrical voltage between these separated charge centres grows strong enough to overcome the insulating resistance of air, electrons surge through a narrow, ionized channel in a giant spark several kilometres long: **lightning**.

A lightning stroke heats its narrow channel of air to roughly 30,000 °C in a few millionths of a second—five times hotter than the surface of the sun. Heated that violently, the air channel explodes outward faster than the speed of sound, launching a supersonic shock wave that quickly relaxes into the booming acoustic wave we hear as **thunder**.[^rumble]

Because light travels at 300,000 kilometres per second, you see the lightning flash the instant it happens. Sound travels through air much more slowly—at about **340 metres per second**—taking roughly **3 seconds to cover a kilometre** (or 5 seconds for a mile). Count the seconds from the flash to the first crack of thunder and divide by 3 to find your distance from the strike in kilometres. (The interactive figure speeds up the clock so you don’t have to wait in real time, while showing the real-world second count.)

blocks.caption: A storm somewhere off over the hills.
blocks.task: Make the storm strike, and count.

blocks.text: Don't assume you are safe just because blue sky sits directly overhead. Because the positively charged upper anvil spreads many kilometres downwind of the dark rain core, a powerful positive lightning bolt can arc out of the high anvil through clear air and strike the ground 10 to 15 kilometres away from the rain shaft—the notorious "bolt from the blue."

That reach is the basis for the **30–30 rule**: if you count **30 seconds or less** between a lightning flash and its thunder, the strike is within 10 kilometres (6 miles) and you are already inside striking range. Seek shelter inside a substantial building or hard-topped vehicle immediately, and stay inside until **30 minutes** after the last rumble of thunder.

After a strong thunderstorm matures, the underside of its spreading anvil sometimes breaks into smooth, rounded pouches hanging toward the ground. The anvil base is loaded with ice crystals and cloud droplets sitting just above much drier clear air. When a pocket of this cloudy anvil air sinks into the dry layer below, its ice crystals and droplets evaporate, absorbing latent heat and chilling the sinking pocket. Because evaporation keeps cooling it from within, the descending cloudy pocket warms at only about 5 °C per kilometre on the way down, whereas the clear air around it warms downward at 6 to 8 °C per kilometre. Remaining colder and denser than the surrounding sky, the pocket keeps sinking in smooth, bulbous lobes—convection running in reverse, powered by evaporation inside sinking air.

blocks.caption: The underside of an anvil, late in a storm.
blocks.task: Let the cold air sink until pouches form.

blocks.text: These pendulous pouches are called **mammatus** (or *mamma*). Lit sideways by low late-afternoon sun, mammatus can look eerie and ominous, leading to a common myth that they signal an imminent tornado. In reality, mammatus lobes are simply sinking, evaporating air under an anvil, most often seen either ahead of a storm or after the worst of the storm has already passed.

blocks.title: Reading storm towers
points: **Morning castle turrets** (*altocumulus castellanus*): the middle floor is already unstable. Watch for afternoon storms.
**Towering cauliflower heaps** (*cumulus congestus*) by midday on a hot, muggy day: thunderstorms likely by mid-afternoon.
**Strong inversion lid** on the morning sounding, or cumulus puffs that stay flat (*humilis*): fair weather will hold.
**Sudden cool, gusty outflow** on a hot afternoon: the storm’s **gust front** has arrived. Get indoors now—rain and lightning are 5 to 15 minutes behind.
**The 30–30 rule**: if flash-to-bang is under 30 seconds (< 10 km), get indoors and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

blocks.text: Compare these photographs side by side, focusing on the visual clue that separates cumulonimbus from its closest look-alikes.

photos.cue: top glaciated into a fibrous anvil

options.tell: Look at the upper edges. Even a towering cumulus congestus keeps crisp, hard-edged cauliflower domes made of liquid droplets. Once the top freezes into soft, silky ice trails and flattens into an anvil, it is cumulonimbus.

From directly underneath, both look dark and wet. Check the horizon and the character of the rain: cumulonimbus is a localized storm tower with brighter sky off to the sides, sudden wind gusts, and intense bursts of rain or thunder. Nimbostratus is a sky-wide blanket bringing hours of steady rain.

blocks.text: First identify the cloud genera in these photographs, then read the forecast from the evolving skies below.

blocks.caption: Real photos to name, then the sky over a few hours. What is it up to?

items.question: When in a thunderstorm’s life does it throw its lightning and downpours?
options: The growing stage, while the updraught is at its very strongest
The dissipating stage, as the storm finally rains itself out
The mature stage, once a downdraught runs beside the updraught
items.why: Growing, the storm is all updraught. The trouble starts when rain and hail drag a downdraught down beside it: that mature stage is when you want everybody under a roof. Dissipating, it is raining itself out.

items.question: On a hot, muggy day, morning cumulus puffs have already swollen into tall, cauliflower congestus towers by noon. What should you expect by mid-afternoon?
options: Thunderstorms (cumulonimbus), as latent heat drives the towers to the tropopause
All-night frontal rain from a lowering altostratus deck
Clearing blue skies, since rapid midday growth uses up the air's moisture
items.why: Cumulus heaps that reach the towering congestus stage by midday show strong instability and ample moisture, often growing into full cumulonimbus thunderstorms by mid-afternoon.

items.question: The morning weather-balloon sounding shows a sharp temperature inversion sitting two kilometres above the ground. How will afternoon cumulus clouds behave today?
options: Explode into severe thunderstorms, fueled by the warm air in the inversion
Flatten out beneath the inversion cap, leaving the day dry
Sink back to the ground and turn into afternoon valley fog
items.why: When rising cumulus tops hit a warmer inversion layer aloft, they become colder and denser than the surrounding air and cannot climb past the cap.

items.question: You see a bright flash of lightning and count 12 seconds before hearing the first boom of thunder. Roughly how far away did the lightning strike?
options: About 1 km (half a mile)
About 4 km (2.5 miles)
About 12 km (7.5 miles)
items.why: Sound travels through air at about 1 kilometre every 3 seconds (1 mile every 5 seconds), so 12 ÷ 3 = 4 km—well inside the 10 km (30-second) danger zone.

items.question: A heavy thunderstorm shower has ended, patches of blue sky are appearing, and the last rumble of thunder was 10 minutes ago. Is it safe to head back out onto the open field?
options: Yes: once the rain stops, the electrical charge has dissipated
Yes, provided the dark cloud base has moved off to the east
Not yet: wait a full 30 minutes after the last thunder before going back outside
items.why: The positively charged upper anvil of a departing thunderstorm can still fire lethal lightning bolts 10 km or more through clear air. Always wait 30 minutes after the final clap of thunder.

items.question: At 7 a.m., you spot a line of middle-floor altocumulus sprouting narrow, castle-like turrets (*castellanus*). What does that tell you about the day ahead?
options: Dry, settled weather: the turrets show the cloud layer is breaking up
Dense radiation fog by evening as the middle layer sinks
A high risk of afternoon thunderstorms, because the middle sky is already unstable
items.why: Altocumulus castellanus reveals that the middle floor is cooling with height faster than the 5 °C/km moist rate, meaning afternoon surface thermals will face no stable cap on their way to becoming thunderstorms.

items.question: On a stifling, calm afternoon, a dark cumulonimbus tower looms to the west. Suddenly the air turns noticeably cool and a gusty wind kicks up dust across the road, though no rain is falling yet. What just reached you?
options: The storm’s gust front: downpours and lightning are 5 to 15 minutes away
The dissipating stage: cool air means the storm has already died out
A warm front: expect 24 hours of gentle, steady drizzle
items.why: Rain-chilled air from the storm's downdraught hits the ground and races ahead of the rain core as a cool, blustery gust front—typically arriving 5 to 15 minutes before the rain and lightning.

learned: Condensing water vapour releases latent heat, slowing a rising cloud parcel's cooling rate from 10 °C/km to about 5 °C/km (3 °F per 1,000 ft). An atmosphere cooling at 6–7 °C/km is stable for dry air but unstable for cloudy air, allowing cumulus towers to accelerate upward once they form.
Cumulus vertical growth progresses from flat humilis (fair weather) to mediocris to towering congestus. Morning altocumulus castellanus turrets warn that the middle floor is already unstable.
On a balloon sounding, temperature runs along the bottom and height up the side; a steeper leftward tilt in the environment curve means faster cooling with height and greater instability.

The tropopause (10–12 km up) is a permanent inversion lid warmed by stratospheric ozone. A storm tower that hits it spreads into a fibrous ice anvil, becoming a cumulonimbus. A single storm cell grows, matures, and dissipates in about an hour.
A sudden blast of cool, gusty wind ahead of a storm is its gust front (outflow from the cold downdraught), arriving 5 to 15 minutes before heavy rain and lightning.

Thunder takes about 3 seconds per kilometre (5 seconds per mile). Under 30 seconds (< 10 km), get indoors and stay inside until 30 minutes after the last thunder (the 30–30 rule). Mammatus pouches under an anvil are harmless sinking, evaporating air.

cumulonimbus.title: Cumulonimbus
cumulonimbus.text: A towering convective cloud that climbs all the way to the tropopause (10–12 km up), where its frozen top flattens and spreads into a fibrous ice anvil. Driven by latent heat released inside strong updraughts, a single cell grows, matures, and dissipates in about an hour, bringing heavy downpours, hail, a cool gust front, and lightning.

lightning.title: Counting the thunder
lightning.text: Collisions between rising ice crystals and falling soft hail (graupel) separate electric charge inside a thunderstorm until a massive spark discharges as lightning, superheating the air channel to ~30,000 °C and launching the shock wave we hear as thunder. Sound travels ~1 km every 3 seconds (1 mile every 5 seconds). The 30–30 rule: if flash-to-bang is under 30 seconds (< 10 km), get indoors and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

mammatus.title: Mammatus
mammatus.text: Smooth, rounded pouches hanging beneath a thunderstorm anvil, formed where pockets of ice- and droplet-laden air sink into drier air below. Evaporating particles chill the sinking pockets so they warm at only ~5 °C/km on the way down, staying colder and denser than their surroundings in upside-down convection. Though dramatic when lit by low sun, mammatus pouches themselves are harmless.

moist-rate.title: Moist adiabatic lapse rate
moist-rate.text: The cooling rate of rising saturated (cloudy) air is the **moist** (or *saturated*) **adiabatic lapse rate**. Unlike the fixed 9.8 °C/km dry rate, the moist rate varies with temperature because warm air holds much more water vapour to condense than cold air does. It ranges from about **4 °C per kilometre** in hot, humid tropical air near the ground to **6–7 °C per kilometre** in the middle sky, and approaches the full 9.8 °C/km dry rate in bitterly cold air near the tropopause. These lessons use **5 °C per kilometre** as a representative lower-to-middle-sky figure.

conditional.title: Conditional instability
conditional.text: When the surrounding atmosphere cools with height at a rate between the moist rate (~5 °C/km) and the dry rate (9.8 °C/km), meteorologists call the sky **conditionally unstable**. The condition is saturation: the layer is stable if a nudged parcel is clear and unsaturated, but becomes unstable *if* the parcel is lifted high enough to condense into cloud.

radiosonde.title: Weather balloons (radiosondes)
radiosonde.text: The shoebox-sized instrument package dangling beneath a weather balloon is a **radiosonde**. Invented in the late 1920s, radiosondes replaced daring early-morning aeroplane flights and giant box kites. Today, roughly 800 stations worldwide launch balloons simultaneously twice every day—at 00:00 and 12:00 UTC. As the balloon climbs into thinning air, it expands from 2 metres wide at launch to the size of a house at 30 km altitude before popping and parachuting its sensor pack back down.

cape.title: CAPE (storm fuel)
cape.text: On a sounding chart, the positive area enclosed between the warmer orange parcel curve and the cooler violet environment curve is proportional to the kinetic energy each kilogram of rising air can gain from buoyancy. Forecasters call this **CAPE** (*Convective Available Potential Energy*), measured in joules per kilogram (J/kg). Values of a few hundred J/kg support ordinary showers; 1,000–2,000 J/kg fuels strong thunderstorms; and 3,000–5,000+ J/kg drives violent supercells with giant hail.

overshooting.title: Overshooting tops
overshooting.text: When a thunderstorm updraught is exceptionally violent—rising at 100 to 150 km/h—its momentum carries the boiling cloud tower a kilometre or two past the tropopause right into the lower stratosphere before gravity pulls the cold, heavy air back down. From the side or from satellite imagery, this looks like a bubbling cauliflower dome poking up out of the flat anvil sheet, called an **overshooting top**—a telltale sign of a severe thunderstorm.

rumble.title: Why thunder rumbles
rumble.text: A lightning stroke lasts only milliseconds, yet its thunder can rumble on for ten seconds or more. That happens because a lightning channel is typically 5 to 10 kilometres long and zigzags across the sky: sound from the nearest segment reaches your ears first as a sharp crack, while sound from segments kilometres further away arrives several seconds later, stretched out further by echoes off hills and clouds.
